case_study_insert.main_stem: Northgate Ceramic Works (NCWK) is a private limited company in the eco-friendly building materials sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2011 by Priya Nandakumar, the business supplies recycled-content ceramic tiles to builders' merchants and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. NCWK plans to invest $720,000 in a new low-emission kiln for recycled-content eco-tiles, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. NCWK faces two problems: the glazing defect rate has reached 4.2% and kiln energy waste is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The eco-tile line fired 25,000 tiles last quarter at a glazing defect rate of 4.2%, down from 6.1% a year ago. Customer complaints about chipped tiles fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 5.6 days. Kiln waste currently runs at 7.5% of output. A survey of 400 builders' merchants found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more per tile for recycled-content eco-tiles, and 57% check environmental credentials before ordering. A training audit shows 18 of 50 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new kiln controls; off-the-job certification courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northgate Ceramic Works for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.10 to $13.87 an hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across the construction supply chain. (3) Wholesale clay and energy input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while building-material inflation is 6.4% and spending on new housing starts grew 2.9%.

questions.question_text: NCWK plans to fund part of its $720,000 low-emission kiln with a $420,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for NCWK of using the $300,000 retained profit instead of borrowing that amount.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit means NCWK pays no interest or capital repayments on that portion of the $720,000 kiln, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year. Every dollar not paid to the lender can absorb the 9.8% rise in clay and energy input costs, so the $14.00 selling price need not be raised and the 4.2% defect-rate problem can be tackled without extra debt pressure.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps control with Priya Nandakumar and the existing shareholders. A bank loan can impose covenants and require collateral, putting the new kiln at risk if demand for recycled-content eco-tiles disappoints; using internally generated funds avoids that risk and preserves the flat, democratic structure, since no outside lender can dictate how the 50-strong workforce is managed or how the $420,000 loan itself is serviced.

The owner-managed culture also means the decision can be taken quickly by Priya Nandakumar without waiting for lender approval, helping NCWK respond to the 9.8% input-cost rise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NCWK's kiln investment, costs and financing mix.

questions.question_text: NCWK is launching recycled-content eco-tiles. Consider advertising in trade magazines, sponsoring a builders' trade exhibition, or running targeted social media campaigns. Which should NCWK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade magazine advertising: Print adverts in builders' journals reach the 400 merchants surveyed and suit a technical product with environmental credentials, with a long shelf life for reference. However, response is slow and hard to measure, and a full-page campaign is costly for a firm funding a $720,000 kiln with a $420,000 bank loan; many readers may never order recycled-content eco-tiles.

Trade exhibition sponsorship: A stand at a national builders' show lets NCWK demonstrate the low-emission kiln output face to face, meet the merchants who care about the 57% environmental-credential finding, and generate immediate orders. The drawbacks are high stand and travel costs and a short event window; with output of 100,000 units a year, one show cannot by itself fill the order book, and the $360,000 fixed costs continue regardless.

Social media campaigns: Targeted campaigns can show the recycled-content story directly to the 68% of surveyed merchants who would pay $0.50 more and the 57% who check credentials, at low cost per contact, with measurable clicks and rapid testing of messages. Reach among traditional builders' merchants may be weaker than print, and results depend on consistent content, but the platform can be scaled nationally as the new kiln ramps up.

Recommendation: NCWK should choose targeted social media campaigns, supported by small leaflets at trade counters. Social media reaches the exact segment identified in the 400-merchant survey at a fraction of exhibition cost and can be measured against tile orders. Trade magazines are rejected as slow, untargeted and expensive for a business servicing a $420,000 loan; exhibitions are rejected because the cost of a single stand is high relative to the 4.2% defect-rate fix and the 100,000-unit output target still needs steady year-round demand.

level_1_1_to_4: Limited awareness of the three promotional options with minimal reference to NCWK.
level_2_5_to_8: Explanation of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to NCWK's research and costs.
level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why magazines and exhibitions are rejected.

questions.question_text: NCWK's glazing defect rate has reached 4.2% and kiln energy waste is rising. Explain two benefits for NCWK of its democratic leadership style in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 50 production staff to help diagnose the 4.2% glazing defect rate, because the operators who fire and glaze the tiles daily often know which kiln settings cause chipping. Involvement raises job satisfaction and ownership (Maslow's esteem needs), so workers are more willing to follow new quality routines, cutting the 44 monthly complaints and reducing the energy waste that arrives with re-fired defective tiles.

Point 2: Because NCWK has a flat structure, ideas from the 18 staff still needing on-the-job training can reach Priya Nandakumar quickly without passing through layers of management. Group discussion of waste measurement gives practical suggestions for the $750-per-person college courses and helps staff accept changes, protecting output of 100,000 units while keeping the $14.00 price and $8.00 variable cost competitive during a 9.8% rise in input costs.

Staff suggestions can also identify which kiln settings waste energy, allowing practical changes that lower the $8.00 variable cost per unit and protect quality without further capital spending.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NCWK's defect rate, waste and flat structure.

questions.question_text: A training audit shows 18 of 50 NCWK production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new kiln controls. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job certification courses at the local college. Which should NCWK choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the kiln is specific to NCWK's own controls and glazing standards, costs no course fees and keeps all 18 staff producing tiles while they learn, which protects the 25,000 tiles fired last quarter and the drive to cut the 4.2% defect rate. It also suits the flat structure, as experienced operators can coach peers. The weaknesses are that trainers' own output suffers, bad habits may be copied, and there is no external certificate to show merchants who check credentials.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per employee would cost $13,500 for 18 staff (18 x $750 = $13,500), affordable beside the $720,000 kiln investment, and gives recognised certification that supports the 57% of surveyed merchants who check environmental credentials. It removes 18 of 50 workers from the line temporarily, however, and generic content may not match NCWK's kiln settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: NCWK should choose on-the-job training first, with short college certification later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while the 4.2% defect rate already strains the 100,000-unit target. Full off-the-job training is rejected because taking 18 of 50 staff off the kiln would disrupt orders and its generic content would not directly reduce glazing defects without further on-site work.

This choice also fits the flat structure: experienced operators can coach the 18 staff alongside their normal duties, and feedback reaches management quickly. NCWK can review defect-rate data after the first quarter and add college certification only where inspection records show a persistent gap.

level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to NCWK.
level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods using NCWK's audit figures and costs.
level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and kiln relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NCWK's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $360,000 ÷ $6.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways the management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units: NCWK has a margin of safety of 40,000 units, showing the eco-tile line is comfortably profitable and can absorb a dip in orders while the new kiln beds in.
2. Use contribution per unit of $6.00 to test pricing: a $0.50 discount would leave $5.50 a unit, still above zero but lowering the cushion over the $360,000 fixed costs, so managers can judge price pressure before agreeing it.
3. Link the 60,000-unit break-even point to the $420,000 bank loan: managers can set a minimum sales target that generates enough contribution to cover fixed costs and interest, testing whether the $720,000 kiln can be serviced from operations.
4. Track average total cost of $11.60 a unit ($360,000 ÷ 100,000 = $3.60 plus $8.00) each quarter to spot the effect of kiln waste and the 9.8% clay and energy inflation, supporting decisions on supplier renegotiation or waste reduction.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 40,000 units against 100,000 output; discount modelling on $6.00 contribution; loan-service volume target for the $420,000 loan; and average total cost benchmarking at $11.60 to tackle waste and 9.8% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NCWK's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed for 2024 and 2025. Has NCWK's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.4%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of 840 on revenue of 2,400 gives 35.0%; 2025 gross profit of 1,120 on revenue of 2,800 gives 40.0%. Operating profit of 288 on revenue of 2,400 gives 12.0% in 2024, and 448 on 2,800 gives 16.0% in 2025. Operating profit of 288 on capital employed of 1,600 gives 18.0% in 2024, and 448 on 2,000 gives 22.4% in 2025. Revenue grew by 400 while cost of sales rose by only 120, and interest payable increased from 36 to 48.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The 35.0% to 40.0% gross margin shows better control of production costs relative to sales, consistent with a premium recycled-content product. The 12.0% to 16.0% operating margin shows operating costs were also controlled, since operating profit rose by 160 while revenue rose by 400. The 18.0% to 22.4% return on capital employed is especially important: the $720,000 kiln investment has not diluted returns, because operating profit grew faster than the capital base. The rise in interest payable from 36 to 48 signals the cost of the $420,000 bank loan, but it has not prevented the improvement.

Conclusion: NCWK's financial performance has improved. Gross margin, operating margin and ROCE all rose, and the improvement is not merely a sales-volume effect. The residual concern is higher interest payable, so management should watch loan costs, but the figures support proceeding with the kiln programme.

level_1_1_to_4: States isolated figures from Appendix 2 with little or no accurate calculation.
level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three measures for both years accurately and describes the trend with some NCWK context.
level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NCWK of producing recycled-content eco-tiles.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled-content eco-tiles match the 68% of 400 surveyed builders' merchants who would pay $0.50 more and the 57% who check environmental credentials. That premium supports the $14.00 selling price and the $6.00 contribution per unit even while clay and energy costs rise 9.8%, and it differentiates NCWK from standard tile suppliers when tendering for environmentally specified housing projects funded through the $420,000 loan.

Disadvantage: Recycled inputs and the low-emission kiln can raise the $8.00 variable cost per unit and complicate quality control; inconsistent recycled feedstock may worsen the current 4.2% glazing defect rate and the 7.5% kiln waste, raising re-firing costs before staff complete the $750 training. If merchants will not accept the full $0.50 premium, margin is squeezed. NCWK must therefore verify that the 68% stated preference converts into actual orders at the new price.

NCWK should therefore test orders at the $0.50 premium before committing more of the $720,000 kiln capacity to recycled-content lines, rather than relying on stated survey intent alone.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using NCWK's survey, costs and defect data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in clay and energy input costs will affect NCWK. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If NCWK's $420,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 x $420,000). That is modest against fixed costs of $360,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the immediate effect is zero. Higher base rates may cool housing starts, which grew only 2.9%, and raise the cost of future borrowing, but NCWK can cap this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.87 an hour): With a workforce of 50, a wage rise feeds into costs that are not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can honestly be invented; the defensible test is productivity. At 100,000 units and 50 staff, output is 2,000 tiles per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost pushes up the $8.00 variable cost and erodes the $6.00 contribution.

Clay and energy input costs (9.8%): This is an illustrative upper bound: if the entire $8.00 variable cost rose 9.8%, that adds $0.78 a unit (0.098 x $8.00 = $0.784), and at 100,000 units that is about $78,400 a year (100,000 x $0.784). Even a smaller pass-through would cut the $6.00 contribution materially. The $0.50 eco-tile premium and supplier negotiation can recover part of it, but the effect reaches every tile sold.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in clay and energy input costs has the greatest impact. It compounds across all 100,000 units and directly attacks the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 kiln, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $3,150 and the wage effect can be offset by productivity. NCWK should prioritise waste reduction and premium pricing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the external factors with minimal application to NCWK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the impact of at least two of the three changes on NCWK's costs, revenue or financing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
